wordings.title: Compress repeated letters
wordings.statement:
Write `compress(text)`.

Replace every run of the same letter with the letter followed by the length of the run:
`"aabcccccaaa"` becomes `"a2b1c5a3"`. If the result is not shorter than `text`, return
`text` unchanged.

Upper and lower case letters are different letters. Aim for linear time.

examples.explanation: "a1b1c1" is longer, so the text stays as it is.

constraints: text holds only letters a-z and A-Z

problems.tests:
from solution import *


def test_example_1():
    """Runs of two, one, five and three letters."""
    assert compress('aabcccccaaa') == 'a2b1c5a3'


def test_example_2():
    """No letter repeats, so the text stays."""
    assert compress('abc') == 'abc'


def test_empty_text():
    """An empty text stays empty."""
    assert compress('') == ''


def test_equal_length_stays():
    """A result of the same length is not shorter."""
    assert compress('aa') == 'aa'
    assert compress('aabb') == 'aabb'


def test_one_long_run():
    """A run longer than nine letters needs a count of several digits."""
    assert compress('a' * 12) == 'a12'
    assert compress('z' * 100000) == 'z100000'


def test_case_matters():
    """Upper and lower case letters form separate runs."""
    assert compress('aaAAA') == 'a2A3'
    assert compress('aAaA') == 'aAaA'


def test_long_text():
    """200,000 letters in runs of four."""
    text = ''.join(letter * 4 for letter in 'abcd' * 12500)
    assert compress(text) == 'a4b4c4d4' * 12500
hints: How do you know where a run ends while you walk through the text once?
Remember where the current run started. When the next letter differs, or the text ends, the run is complete: write its letter and length.
Collect the pieces in a list and join them once at the end: adding to a string piece by piece can copy it every time. Compare the lengths before returning.
problems.summary: Run-length encode a string, keeping the original when encoding does not shorten it

wordings.title: Reverse a linked list
wordings.statement:
A node of a singly linked list has a `value` and a `next` node; the last node's `next`
is `null`.

Write `reverse(head)`. It reverses the list in place, by changing the `next` links of
the existing nodes, and returns the new head. An empty list is given as `null`.

Use constant extra memory.

problems.tests:
from solution import *


def _build(values):
    head = None
    for value in reversed(values):
        head = Node(value, head)
    return head


def _nodes(head):
    nodes = []
    while head is not None:
        nodes.append(head)
        head = head.next
    return nodes


def _values(head):
    return [node.value for node in _nodes(head)]


def test_example_1():
    """Three nodes come back in the opposite order."""
    assert _values(reverse(_build([1, 2, 3]))) == [3, 2, 1]


def test_example_2():
    """An empty list stays empty."""
    assert reverse(None) is None


def test_one_node():
    """A single node is its own reverse."""
    node = Node(7)
    assert reverse(node) is node
    assert node.next is None


def test_same_nodes():
    """The list is reversed in place: the nodes are reused, not copied."""
    head = _build([1, 2, 3, 4])
    before = _nodes(head)
    assert _nodes(reverse(head)) == before[::-1]


def test_old_head_ends_the_list():
    """The old head becomes the last node."""
    head = _build([5, 6])
    reverse(head)
    assert head.next is None


def test_long_list():
    """1,000 nodes."""
    values = list(range(1000))
    assert _values(reverse(_build(values))) == values[::-1]
hints: While you walk the list, what do you need to remember so that no node is lost when you change its `next`?
Keep the previous node. For each node, save its `next`, point it at the previous node, then move on.

Start with previous = null. Repeat: next_node = node.next; node.next = previous; previous = node; node = next_node. When node is null, previous is the new head. A recursive version uses memory for every node.
problems.summary: Reverse a singly linked list in place by turning each next link around

wordings.title: First letter that appears once
wordings.statement:
Write `first_unique(text)` that returns the index of the first character in `text` that
appears exactly once, or `-1` when every character repeats.

Aim for linear time.

hints: To know that a character appears once, you need its count over the whole text. Can you get every count in one pass?
Count the characters in a hash map in a first pass. A second pass finds the first character whose count is 1.
Two passes of n steps each are still linear. Checking every character against the rest of the text instead is quadratic.
problems.summary: Find the first non-repeating character with a count per character

wordings.title: Stack with a minimum
wordings.statement:
Write a class `MinStack` with these methods:

- `push(value)` puts `value` on top
- `pop()` removes the top value and returns it
- `top()` returns the top value without removing it
- `get_min()` returns the smallest value on the stack

Every method must take constant time. `pop`, `top` and `get_min` are only called on a
stack that is not empty.

examples.input: push(3), push(1), push(2), get_min(), pop(), pop(), get_min()
examples.explanation: After 2 and 1 are popped, only 3 is left.

constraints: Values are integers and may repeat

problems.tests:
from solution import *


def test_example_1():
    """The minimum returns to 3 once 1 is popped."""
    stack = MinStack()
    stack.push(3)
    stack.push(1)
    stack.push(2)
    assert stack.get_min() == 1
    assert stack.pop() == 2
    assert stack.pop() == 1
    assert stack.get_min() == 3


def test_top_does_not_remove():
    """top() shows the last value and leaves it there."""
    stack = MinStack()
    stack.push(5)
    stack.push(8)
    assert stack.top() == 8
    assert stack.top() == 8
    assert stack.pop() == 8
    assert stack.top() == 5


def test_repeated_minimum():
    """Popping one copy of the minimum leaves the other."""
    stack = MinStack()
    for value in [2, 1, 1]:
        stack.push(value)
    stack.pop()
    assert stack.get_min() == 1
    stack.pop()
    assert stack.get_min() == 2


def test_negative_values():
    """Negative values are smaller."""
    stack = MinStack()
    stack.push(0)
    stack.push(-4)
    assert stack.get_min() == -4


def test_reuse_after_empty():
    """A stack emptied and filled again forgets its old minimum."""
    stack = MinStack()
    stack.push(1)
    stack.pop()
    stack.push(9)
    assert stack.get_min() == 9


def test_many_calls():
    """100,000 pushes, each followed by get_min, then pops back down."""
    stack = MinStack()
    for value in range(100000, 0, -1):
        stack.push(value)
        assert stack.get_min() == value
    for value in range(1, 100001):
        assert stack.get_min() == value
        assert stack.pop() == value
hints: Searching the stack for its minimum takes linear time. What could you store at push time so that the minimum is always known?
The minimum only changes when a value is pushed or popped. Store, with every value, the minimum of the stack at the moment it was pushed.
Push (value, min(value, minimum below)). pop() and top() read the value of the top entry, get_min() its stored minimum.
problems.summary: Stack that returns its minimum in constant time by storing the running minimum

wordings.title: Queue from two stacks
wordings.statement:
Write a class `StackQueue`, a first-in first-out queue built from two stacks. A stack
here is a list used only at its end: push a value at the end, pop the last value, read
the last value.

- `enqueue(value)` adds `value` at the back
- `dequeue()` removes the front value and returns it
- `peek()` returns the front value without removing it
- `size()` returns the number of values

Any sequence of n calls must take O(n) time in total. `dequeue` and `peek` are only
called on a queue that is not empty.

examples.input: enqueue(1), enqueue(2), dequeue(), enqueue(3), dequeue(), size()

problems.tests:
from solution import *


def test_example_1():
    """Values leave in the order they arrived."""
    queue = StackQueue()
    queue.enqueue(1)
    queue.enqueue(2)
    assert queue.dequeue() == 1
    queue.enqueue(3)
    assert queue.dequeue() == 2
    assert queue.size() == 1


def test_empty_size():
    """A new queue holds nothing."""
    assert StackQueue().size() == 0


def test_peek_does_not_remove():
    """peek() shows the front value and leaves it there."""
    queue = StackQueue()
    queue.enqueue('a')
    queue.enqueue('b')
    assert queue.peek() == 'a'
    assert queue.size() == 2
    assert queue.dequeue() == 'a'
    assert queue.peek() == 'b'


def test_interleaved():
    """Values added after some were taken still wait their turn."""
    queue = StackQueue()
    out = []
    for value in range(10):
        queue.enqueue(value)
        if value % 3 == 2:
            out.append(queue.dequeue())
    while queue.size():
        out.append(queue.dequeue())
    assert out == list(range(10))


def test_many_calls():
    """100,000 values pass through, taken in batches."""
    queue = StackQueue()
    out = []
    for value in range(100000):
        queue.enqueue(value)
        if value % 1000 == 999:
            for _ in range(500):
                out.append(queue.dequeue())
    while queue.size():
        out.append(queue.dequeue())
    assert out == list(range(100000))
hints: Popping every value from one stack and pushing it onto another reverses their order. How does that help a queue?
Push new values onto an incoming stack. Take values from an outgoing stack; when it is empty, move everything from incoming into it.
Each value is moved at most once from incoming to outgoing, so n calls cost O(n) in total although a single dequeue can be slow. size() is the sum of both lengths.
problems.summary: First-in first-out queue from two stacks with amortized constant time per call

wordings.title: Is it a binary search tree?
wordings.statement:
A tree node has a `value`, a `left` child and a `right` child; a missing child is
`null`.

Write `is_search_tree(root)` that returns `true` when the tree is a binary search tree:
for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller than its value and all values
in its right subtree are larger. An empty tree, given as `null`, is a search tree.

examples.input: root = 5 with left 1 and right 6, where 6 has left 4 and right 7
examples.explanation: 4 is in the right subtree of 5 but smaller than 5.

constraints: The tree is at most 20 levels deep
Values are integers; a repeated value makes the tree not a search tree

hints: Is it enough to compare every node with its own children? Look at the second example.
Each node must lie between bounds set by its ancestors: going left sets an upper bound, going right a lower bound.
Recurse with (node, low, high). The root has no bounds. A node fails if its value is not strictly between low and high; its left child gets (low, value), its right child (value, high).
problems.summary: Validate a binary search tree by passing value bounds down from the ancestors

wordings.title: Merge sorted lists
wordings.statement:
Write `merge_sorted(lists)`. `lists` holds k lists of integers, each sorted in ascending
order. Return one ascending list with every value from all of them, repeats included.

With n values in total, aim for O(n log k) time.
constraints: Any of the lists may be empty

problems.reference_solution:
import heapq


def merge_sorted(lists):
    """Return one ascending list with all values of the ascending lists."""
    heap = [(values[0], i, 0) for i, values in enumerate(lists) if values]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    merged = []
    while heap:
        value, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
        merged.append(value)
        if j + 1 < len(lists[i]):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (lists[i][j + 1], i, j + 1))
    return merged
problems.tests:
import random

from solution import *


def test_example_1():
    """Three lists woven together."""
    assert merge_sorted([[1, 4, 7], [2, 5], [3, 6, 9]]) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9]


def test_example_2():
    """An empty list next to a list of one."""
    assert merge_sorted([[], [1]]) == [1]


def test_no_lists():
    """Nothing to merge."""
    assert merge_sorted([]) == []
    assert merge_sorted([[], []]) == []


def test_repeats_are_kept():
    """Equal values from different lists all appear."""
    assert merge_sorted([[1, 1, 2], [1, 2]]) == [1, 1, 1, 2, 2]


def test_negative_values():
    """Negative values come first."""
    assert merge_sorted([[-5, 0], [-7, 3]]) == [-7, -5, 0, 3]


def test_inputs_unchanged():
    """The given lists are not changed."""
    lists = [[1, 3], [2]]
    merge_sorted(lists)
    assert lists == [[1, 3], [2]]


def test_many_lists():
    """2,000 lists with 200,000 values in total."""
    rng = random.Random(7)
    lists = [sorted(rng.randrange(-10**6, 10**6) for _ in range(100)) for _ in range(2000)]
    expected = sorted(value for values in lists for value in values)
    assert merge_sorted(lists) == expected
hints: The next value of the result is the smallest among the first remaining values of the lists. How can you find that quickly when there are many lists?
Keep one entry per list in a min-heap: its current value and where it came from. The top of the heap is always the next value.
Pop the smallest entry, append its value, and push the next value of the same list if it has one. Each of the n values is pushed and popped once, at O(log k) each.
problems.summary: Merge k sorted lists with a min-heap holding the front of each list

wordings.text: A dynamic array doubles its capacity whenever it is full, copying its elements into the new space. What is the cost of one append, averaged over many appends?

questions.explanation:
A copy of n elements happens only after n appends since the last one, so the copies add
up to less than 2n over n appends. The average, the amortized cost, is constant; a single
append that triggers a copy costs O(n).
questions.summary: Amortized cost of appending to a doubling array

wordings.text: An array holds n elements in consecutive memory. What does inserting a new element at index 0 cost?

questions.explanation:
Every existing element moves one place to the right to make room, which is n moves.
Inserting at the end needs no moves; a linked list or a deque inserts at the front in
O(1).
questions.summary: Cost of inserting at the front of an array

wordings.text: Strings are immutable. A loop builds a string of n characters by doing `s = s + c` once per character. What does the whole loop cost in the worst case?

questions.explanation:
Each step can copy the whole string built so far: 1 + 2 + … + n characters, which is
O(n²). Collecting the pieces in a list, or a string builder, and joining them once is
O(n). Some runtimes optimise this case, but it is not guaranteed.
questions.summary: Cost of building a string by repeated concatenation

wordings.text: Two strings are anagrams when they hold the same characters with the same counts. Which checks tell correctly whether two strings are anagrams?
options: Sort the characters of both and compare the results
Count the characters of each in a hash map and compare the counts
Compare the sets of characters of both
Compare their lengths and their first and last characters

questions.explanation:
Sorting gives O(n log n) and counting O(n); both compare every character with its count.
Sets lose the counts: "aab" and "abb" have the same set. Lengths and ends say nothing
about the middle.
questions.summary: Correct ways to check that two strings are anagrams

wordings.text: Two pointers start at the head of a singly linked list. One moves one node per step, the other two nodes per step. Where is the slower pointer when the faster one reaches the end?
options: In the middle of the list

questions.explanation:
The fast pointer covers twice the distance, so when it has walked the whole list the
slow one has walked half of it. This finds the middle in one pass without knowing the
length.
questions.summary: Finding the middle of a linked list with a slow and a fast pointer

wordings.text: How can you tell whether a singly linked list contains a cycle, using O(1) extra memory?
options: Move a slow and a fast pointer; they meet only if there is a cycle
Walk until a node's next is null and count the steps
Store every visited node in a hash set
Compare every node's value with the value of the head

questions.summary: Detecting a cycle in a linked list in constant memory

wordings.text: What must be true of keys for a hash map to find them reliably?
options: A key's hash does not change while the key is in the map

questions.explanation:
The map looks in the slot given by the hash, so equal keys must land in the same slot,
and a key whose hash changes is looked for in the wrong slot. Different keys may share a
hash: that is a collision, which the map handles. Any type with a hash and equality can
be a key.
questions.summary: Rules a hash map key must follow

wordings.text: A hash map with n keys is unlucky: every key has the same hash. What does a lookup cost in a map that chains colliding keys in a list?

questions.explanation:
All keys sit in one chain, which is searched element by element. The O(1) of a hash map
is the expected cost with a hash function that spreads keys evenly.
questions.summary: Lookup cost when every key collides

wordings.text: You push 1, 2 and 3 onto an empty stack, then pop twice. Which values come out, in order?

questions.explanation:
A stack is last in, first out: 3 was pushed last and comes out first, then 2. A queue
would give 1, 2.
questions.summary: Order in which a stack returns its values

wordings.text: Which tasks does a stack fit naturally?
options: Checking that brackets in a text are correctly nested
Undoing the most recent edits first
Serving customers in the order they arrived
Evaluating an expression in postfix notation, such as 3 4 + 2 ×

questions.explanation:
Brackets, undo and postfix evaluation all deal first with the most recent item that is
still open. Serving in arrival order is first in, first out: a queue.
questions.summary: Tasks that suit a stack

wordings.text: Breadth-first search visits nodes level by level from the start. Which structure holds the nodes waiting to be visited?

questions.explanation:
A queue hands out nodes in the order they were found, so all nodes one step away come
before those two steps away. A stack instead gives depth-first order.
questions.summary: Structure that drives breadth-first search

wordings.text: The maximum of every window of k consecutive values can be found in O(n) by keeping candidate indices in a deque. Which operations must the deque do in O(1)?
options: Add and remove at both ends
Insert a value in sorted position
Remove an element from the middle

questions.explanation:
New indices join at the back after smaller values are dropped from the back, and indices
that leave the window are dropped from the front. A deque does both ends in O(1); the
other operations are not needed.
questions.summary: Operations a deque provides in constant time

wordings.text: Which traversal of a binary search tree visits its values in ascending order?

questions.explanation:
In-order visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. In a search tree
everything on the left is smaller and everything on the right is larger, so the values
come out sorted.
questions.summary: Traversal that lists a search tree in order

wordings.text: A binary tree has n nodes. Which describes its height, the number of levels?
options: At least about log₂ n and at most n

questions.explanation:
A complete tree packs 2ᵏ nodes into level k, so it needs only about log₂ n levels. A tree
where every node has one child is a chain of n levels. Search and insert cost depends on
the height, which is why balanced trees matter.
questions.summary: Smallest and largest height of a binary tree

wordings.text: Values are inserted one by one into a binary search tree that does not rebalance. Which insertion order makes a search cost O(n)?
options: Middle value first, then the middles of each half
Any order: search always costs O(log n)

questions.explanation:
Each new value is larger than all before it and goes to the right of the last one: the
tree is a chain. Random order gives a height of O(log n) on average, and middle-first
order gives a balanced tree.
questions.summary: Insertion order that degrades a search tree to a list

wordings.text: To check that a binary tree is a search tree, you check that each node's left child is smaller than it and its right child larger. Why is that not enough?
options: A node deeper down can be on the wrong side of an ancestor
It misses nodes with only one child

questions.explanation:
In 5 → right 6 → left 4, each child is on the right side of its parent, yet 4 is in the
right subtree of 5. Each node must lie between bounds set by all its ancestors.
questions.summary: Why comparing with children does not validate a search tree

wordings.text: A binary min-heap holds n values. What do reading the minimum and removing the minimum cost?
options: O(1) to read, O(log n) to remove
O(log n) to read, O(log n) to remove
O(1) to read, O(1) to remove
O(1) to read, O(n) to remove

questions.explanation:
The minimum is always at the root. Removing it moves the last value to the root and sifts
it down one level at a time, and the heap has O(log n) levels.
questions.summary: Costs of reading and removing the top of a heap

wordings.text: You need the k largest of n values that arrive one at a time, using O(k) memory. What do you keep?
options: A min-heap of the k largest so far, replacing its top when a larger value arrives
A max-heap of all values seen
A sorted array of all values seen
A queue of the last k values

questions.explanation:
The top of the min-heap is the smallest of the current k largest: a new value either
beats it and replaces it, in O(log k), or is ignored. Keeping all values needs O(n)
memory, and the last k values are not the largest.
questions.summary: Keeping the k largest values of a stream

wordings.text: A graph has V vertices and E edges, with E much smaller than V². Which representation needs O(V + E) memory?
options: A V × V table of distances
An incidence matrix of V rows and E columns

questions.explanation:
An adjacency list stores each vertex once and each edge in the lists of its ends. The
matrix and the distance table use V² cells whatever the number of edges, and the incidence
matrix V × E.
questions.summary: Representation that suits a sparse graph

wordings.text: Which representation answers "is there an edge from u to v?" in O(1) time?
options: An adjacency list that keeps each vertex's neighbours in an array
A single list of all edges
A list of the vertices in breadth-first order

questions.explanation:
The matrix cell at row u, column v holds the answer. An adjacency list scans u's
neighbours, O(degree of u), and an edge list scans all E edges. Keeping neighbours in a
hash set instead also answers in O(1) on average.
questions.summary: Representation with a constant-time edge check
